The Missing Layer in AI-Assisted Research

John Koblinsky developed the Evidence Assurance framework — a practical way to know how much trust to place in AI-generated insights.

August 2026 · 5 min read

John Koblinsky loaded 28 interview transcripts into an AI research platform — transcripts from a messaging study he'd run himself, interviews he'd sat in on, findings he'd written up by hand. He asked a simple question: which messages performed best with buyers? The AI gave him a confident answer. It was wrong.

John Koblinsky

Director of Research and Insights, SAP Concur
20+ years in market research · Former Microsoft, Amazon, Reckitt, MetLife

Koblinsky only caught the error because he'd also done the laborious work manually. The AI platform processed a subset of his transcripts, produced some high-level thematic feedback, and returned a verdict — without flagging what it had actually read. Most stakeholders would have taken the answer at face value.

This wasn't an isolated incident. He tested the same use case with three other enterprise-grade AI tools. All failed in similar ways. The outputs looked authoritative, read with confidence, and provided no indication of their actual evidentiary foundation.

"A finding that can't tell you how confident to be is little more than a gut feeling — or, with AI, potentially a hallucination."
— John Koblinsky

The Framework: Three Levels of Evidence Assurance

The market research industry spent 80 years developing methodological discipline — sample sizes, margins of error, confidence intervals — so that findings could be trusted. AI bypasses that discipline. The output looks the same whether it's built on 200 interviews or invented on the spot. LLMs present both in the same confident voice.

Koblinsky's response was to build what he calls Evidence Assurance — a framework that describes how much trust to place in AI-generated research based on how directly an answer can be traced to the evidence underneath it.

The Three Levels

Directional

Useful guidance, but the evidence chain is incomplete. Good for exploration, pattern recognition, fast synthesis. Not for decisions that require proof.

Grounded

Answer is based on retrieved research evidence. Tied to specific sources with moderate traceability. Materially stronger than directional.

Auditable

Fully traceable to primary evidence. The receipts are available. You can verify the claim against the source material.

Why This Matters for PMMs

Here's what product marketers should notice: the evidence problem cuts both ways.

If you're using AI to synthesize competitive intelligence — and you should be — you need Koblinsky's framework to evaluate the output. Is this ChatGPT response directional, grounded, or auditable? Can you trace this claim back to something real?

But there's a flip side that matters just as much. When buyers use AI to research your product, the same evidence problem applies in reverse. Is YOUR content auditable? When Claude or Perplexity or a Copilot agent answers a question about your category, can it trace its response back to specific, verifiable claims from your site?

The Input Problem

Evaluating AI Output

When you use AI for research, apply Evidence Assurance to assess how much you can trust what you're getting back.

The Output Problem

Your Content as Evidence

When buyers use AI to research you, your content becomes the evidence. Vague claims give AI nothing to cite.

Directional Content

Adjectives Without Proof

"Industry-leading" and "best-in-class" are directional. AI can't cite them — it either hedges or moves on.

Auditable Content

Named Outcomes

"Accenture reduced cycle times 40%" is auditable. Named customer, specific outcome, verifiable claim.

The Practical Application

Koblinsky built Evidence Assurance to help researchers evaluate AI output. But it translates directly into a content audit for PMMs:

  • Inventory your claims. List the key assertions on your product pages, feature descriptions, and competitive content.
  • Apply the framework. Is each claim directional (adjectives and positioning), grounded (citable facts), or auditable (named outcomes with evidence)?
  • Close the gaps. For every directional claim that matters, find the grounded fact. For every grounded fact, find the auditable proof.
  • Make evidence indexable. Customer outcomes buried in PDF case studies don't help AI cite you. The evidence needs to be on pages that crawlers can read.

The goal isn't to replace marketing with a spec sheet. It's to ensure that when AI encounters your content — and it will, increasingly — there's something auditable underneath the positioning.

The Shared Standard

Content marketing spent 20 years optimizing for Google — keywords, metadata, backlinks — and now the ground is shifting. AI doesn't care about your keyword density. It cares about whether you gave it something it can cite without looking stupid.

The evidence problem really does cut both ways. Evaluate AI's claims with the Evidence Assurance framework. And make sure your own content passes the same test.
